newsitem.title: VATICAN: Castro says Pope will get king's welcome in Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Castro says Pope will get king's welcome in Cuba.

text.p: Pope John Paul on Tuesday accepted an "unconditional" invitation from President Fidel Castro to visit communist Cuba next year and the Cuban leader said the Pontiff would be treated "like a king".
The Pope accepted Castro's invitation during a historic first meeting beteen the veteran revolutionary and the Catholic leader who encouraged Eastern Europeans to shake off communism.
"He will be received like a king and with respect," Castro told a news conference after the 35-minute audience.
Castro, wearing a dark suit, was whisked into the Vatican in a motorcade of 16 cars, one with a light machine gun poking through its sunroof.
It was some of the tightest security ever seen in Rome.
"Holy Father, I hope to see you in Cuba soon," chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls quoted Castro as saying at the end their meeting in the Pope's frescoed private study.
The Pope replied: "Thank you, my blessings on the Cuban people."
The Pope and Castro, both major figures in 20th century history, talked privately in Spanish during the audience.
"Holy Father, this is a great honour for me," Castro, who was schooled by the Jesuits as a child, told the Pope as they met on the threshold of the papal study.
Talking to Vatican officials during a lunch following the audience, Castro called it a "miracle" and thanked the Vatican for its opposition to the long-standing U.S. embargo of the communist nation.
Both Castro and the Vatican said there would be no conditions attached to the trip, the Pope's first to Cuba, the only Spanish-speaking Latin American country he has not visited.
"I did not put any conditions on the Pope and the Pope did not put any conditions on me either," Castro said.
Navarro-Valls would not be drawn on whether Castro and the Polish-born Pope, one of the key influences on the fall of communism in eastern Europe, had discussed human rights issues.
A statement said that Castro discussed political issues with Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Angelo Sodano.

His visit, though billed as private, had all the trappings of a state visit to the Vatican including a 25-minute tour of St Peter's Basilica, Christendom's largest church. Castro also admired Michelangelo's frescoes in the Vatican's Sistine Chapel.
Castro told the news conference that the meeting with the Pope "had a strong impact on me" and that he had "always appreciated the teachings of Jesus Christ".
Navarro-Valls said most of the audience between the Pope and Castro dealt with the role of the Roman Catholic Church in Cuba, where relations with the state have been sometimes frosty.
"They examined questions concerning the normalisation of the conditions of existence of the Church in Cuba and in general the role of believers in Cuban national life," the spokesman said.
Castro said the Cuban government was prepared to work with the Church for the common good.

Shortly after Castro took control in 1959, Cuba was declared a socialist state. Some 350 Catholic schools were nationalised and more than 100 priests expelled. Freedom of worship and religious instruction are limited to church premises.
All media access for the meeting, the Pope's most significant since he received then Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev in December 1989, was cancelled at an hour's notice.
